title: Avoiding other arrangers' ideas and praying for his own
summary: Asked about influences like Challis, Ellington and Redman, he says he listens to other arrangements only to get away from them and prays for his ideas.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Well, in your arranging, you don't seem to have been influenced by any of the arrangers that most of us know about, like Ellington or Fletcher Henderson, Don Redman. Who was your influence? Did you ever hear any of the arrangements that Bill Challis made?
He arranged for the Whitman band and Goldkette's Gene Coyat's band and --

Bill -- as a matter of fact, I don't think I know the name, but I heard those bands. They played some very good arrangements. But, now, for instance, say if you had a band and you wanted me to make an arrangement -- let's just say, if you wanted me to make -- say, I want you to make me a knockout arrangement on 'Poor Butterfly'.
Well, what I would do, I'd say, you want me to make a knockout arrangement on 'Poor Butterfly'. I would try to see if I could hear two or three arrangements on 'Poor Butterfly'.
Now, when I hear those arrangements, not to extract anything, but to get away from them.
To see what had been done.

Yeah. I don't want to do nothing that they've been doing, because I wouldn't want you to say, well, Randolph, you copied such-and-such-such a guy's style. I don't want that style. I want to do something entirely new. I've always tried to stay away from the other arranger, see. Not that I didn't respect the man's arranging and ability, and respect his motivations and creations and what have you, but I would always make it my business to try to stay away from the other arrangers. And that, by doing that, why, it puts you in more of a creative vein, and you don't become lazy up here.

If you begin to say, oh, well, I'll just pick up eight measures, what he's doing, and so on and so on, I just have to put that down, well, what have I done for this? Nothing.

You see. I haven't done anything for my brain. So, one guy asked me, he says, "Randolph, how do you manage to put so much blankety-blank in your arrangements?" You know, what you leave in there. That's what he called it, see. Blankety-blank. I say, I pray for it. I say, I pray, I ask a nice God to give me my ideas, things like that. And they come, pouring.
